title: You start seeing the blocks with your eyes shut.
description:
You start seeing the blocks with your eyes shut. Falling, turning, slotting into gaps, right at the edge of sleep. Harvard researchers put numbers on it in 2000: 17 of 27 players reported the same images.

His team trained volunteers on Tetris for three days and woke them at sleep onset. The reports were eerily alike: everyone saw pieces falling, nobody saw the score, the board, or the keyboard.

Amnesiacs saw the blocks too, with no memory of the game. Five patients with hippocampal damage could not recall playing. Three still saw falling pieces as they dozed. One sat down and set her fingers on the right keys, not knowing why.

The dream came without the memory that should carry it. The pictures surfaced even when the conscious record of the day was gone: evidence that sleep-onset imagery runs on a different memory system than the one that recalls events.

The players who needed to learn the most were the ones who dreamed of it most.

Sources:
- https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11030656/: PubMed record for Stickgold, Malia, Maguire, Roddenberry & O'Connor, 'Replaying the game: hypnagogic images in normals and amnesics,' Science 2000 Oct 13;290(5490):350-353, read directly. Establishes: participants playing Tetris reported intrusive, stereotypical visual images of the game at sleep onset; three amnesic patients with extensive bilateral medial temporal lobe damage produced similar hypnagogic reports despite being unable to recall playing, suggesting the imagery can arise without the declarative memory system; and control participants reported images from previously played versions, showing remote memories can shape the imagery. Lead-author affiliation: Harvard Medical School.
- https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/tetris-dreams/: Scientific American (Kristin Leutwyler, 16 Oct 2000), read in full. Gives the participant breakdown: 27 subjects total (12 novices; 10 experts with 50-500 prior hours; 5 amnesiacs), trained over three days; 17 of the 27 reported the sleep-onset images; three of the five amnesiacs did, most of whom did not remember the game day to day; co-author David Roddenberry observed one amnesiac place her fingers on the correct keys without knowing why; all reports were of falling/rotating pieces, none of the score, board or keyboard; and the novices initially worst at the game reported the images most.
